prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, in which many neutral atoms are held at a magic wavelength, opening a new regime of accuracy and stability in the measurement of time and frequency

statement.case_for: I keep the two-name optical lattice clock prize. After round 1 the case rests on three things I can check against experiment. First, the concept: choosing the trap wavelength so that the light shift is identical for both clock levels removes the old trade-off between long interrogation and perturbation by the trap, and it allows thousands of atoms to be interrogated in parallel. That is a new principle for neutral atoms, not a better version of the single-ion scheme. Second, reproduction: independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE and others) report systematic uncertainties near 1e-18 and their cross-comparisons agree, which is the standard I apply to any measurement claim. Third, the measurements it has enabled: gravitational redshift resolved over millimetres, bounds on drifting constants and ultralight dark matter with stated uncertainties, and the technical basis for a redefinition of the second. The credit is the cleanest on the shortlist: Katori for the scheme and the first lattice clock, Ye for taking accuracy, stability and many-body control to the frontier. I have thought about a second part, and I do not see one: the credited names would have to fit within three people in total, and B047 already uses two.
statement.case_against: The objection that has not gone away, and that Danielsson, Olsson, Mehlig and Johansson all raise in one form or another, is that the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes already recognised the toolbox, and that so far the fundamental-physics output is limits rather than a signal. The redefinition of the second has not happened, so a prize now precedes its most visible consequence. B006 has the broadest ballot support and a prediction-then-experiment structure that is a clearer discovery in the conventional sense, although its third name (Hasan or Mele) and the missing Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang are unresolved. Credit is also left out for lattice-clock groups such as SYRTE and the Yb groups. If a majority of the committee holds that only a new phenomenon qualifies, I would accept B006 as the better choice and would not regard that as a poor outcome.

responses.point: Danielsson regards the lattice clocks as a magnificent instrument but not a discovery, because the output so far is upper limits, and he says his view would change quickly with a redefinition of the second or a dark-matter signal.
responses.response: I accept your test, where is the clue from nature, but I think it is met in part already. The millimetre-scale gravitational redshift measured across a cloud of atoms and the 1e-18 agreement between independent clocks are positive measurements of a relativistic effect at a scale that no earlier instrument reached, and the limits on constant drift and ultralight dark matter come from the same data. I do not make the redefinition a precondition: it is a metrological decision driven by international agreement and by the readiness of several clocks, and it will follow the physics, not define it. What I concede is wording. The citation should name the magic-wavelength lattice and the accuracy and stability it made reachable, and should not say precision measurement in general. Where we still differ is whether a new instrument concept that opens measurement ranges counts as a discovery. For me, in the Swedish tradition of recognising methods, it does.

responses.point: Olsson finds B047 well verified and cleanly attributed and close to the tools-that-open-doors criterion, but asks whether the redefinition of the second is a precondition, and says B047 would rank above B038 or B022 if it is not.
responses.response: Thank you for asking directly. My answer is that it is not a precondition. The prize would recognise the lattice scheme and the accuracy it enabled, and that rests on measurements already done and cross-checked, whereas the redefinition depends on the comparison campaigns and on the choice among several candidate transitions and species, which could take years and may not select the lattice at all. Waiting for it would tie the prize to a decision outside physics. On your condition that B006 is acceptable only if Mele's contribution is clarified, I cannot judge the 2005 papers better than a theorist can. As an experimentalist I would only say that the HgTe edge-conductance measurement is what turned a model into a material fact, so that is where I would keep B006's weight if the committee goes that way.

responses.point: Mehlig regards the clock case as strong on maturity and attribution but does not see it as opening a new class of phenomena the way topological insulators did, and would not object to it as a second part of a two-achievement prize.
responses.response: I think the clock work does open a class, namely tests of relativity and fundamental physics by direct frequency comparison between many atoms at separations of millimetres, but I recognise that this is a statement of reach and not a new state of matter. On your suggestion of a two-part prize, I looked at pairing with B006 or B017. The three-person ceiling is the problem: Katori and Ye already take two names, leaving one for the other part, and there is no honest one-person B006 or B017. A two-part configuration would either split Kane and Molenkamp or remove Katori or Ye, which would damage the cleanest credit on our list. So I would keep single-part configurations, and I agree with you that B006 is the right comparison, and I have kept it as my first alternative.

responses.point: Lindroth would hold at two names for B047, because adding a SYRTE or Yb name invites a priority dispute that cannot be settled from the files, and treats the 2005 and 2012 overlap as shared uncertainty.
responses.response: On reflection I agree with you and I am withdrawing my open question about a third name. Katori and Ye are traceable to the scheme and to the accuracy records, and a third name from SYRTE or the Yb groups would be a choice among several equally real contributions with no basis in the files for ranking them. I do not want the citation to depend on that choice. I also take your suggestion of wording the citation around the trapped atoms at a magic wavelength, and have put that into mine. Where I would still ask for caution is your idea of centring it on the relativistic redshift: that is a spectacular demonstration, but it is a consequence of the accuracy, and a citation built on one application would date quickly if the second is redefined or a dark-matter bound turns into something else.

responses.point: Pearce frames the choice as B006, with the widest ballot support but an unresolved third name, against B047 with narrower support and a clean credit, and asks whether the 2005 and 2012 prizes make a lattice-clock prize look incremental.
responses.response: I would not let ballot counts decide the question, and you say as much yourself. Seven rankings for B006 reflect a diffuse agreement that the field is important, while the disagreement about who the three should be (Hasan or Mele) is a scientific disagreement about what the discovery is. B047 has a shorter list of supporters, but they all name the same two people and the same experimental basis. On incrementalism, I would distinguish: the comb gave the means to count optical cycles, the ion work gave quantum control of one particle, and the lattice clock combined a new trapping principle with parallel interrogation of many atoms. Without the magic wavelength the stability of the best clocks today would not be reachable. I would change my order if the committee could show me that Hall and Hänsch's and Wineland's citations already cover that, but I do not think they do. I also agree with your point on B048: I would leave it for a later cycle.

responses.point: Johansson prefers circuit QED as a distinct discovery (strong light-matter coupling on a chip and dispersive readout) and has disclosed his institutional ties to the topic.
responses.response: I keep B038 as an alternative, and I appreciate that you flagged your interest openly. My view is that dispersive readout is a real measurement method and that the 2004 strong-coupling proposal and its experimental demonstration are distinct from the macroscopic tunnelling that was honoured in 2025. What holds me back is the missing Girvin and Huang from the credit, which the chair's summary lists as acknowledged by five of us, and the closeness in time to a prize in the same technology. I would put B038 in front of the committee more readily after a few years. I also note my own link to WACQT in my disclosure, so you should weigh my reasoning on B038 on its merits and not on the basis of my institutional neighbourhood.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, given that Danielsson, Mehlig and Olsson continue to doubt it.
I have not independently checked the latest published uncertainty records or the exact Sr and Yb priority history, and I rely on the round-1 statements for those.
Whether a prize that precedes the redefinition of the second could look premature, or alternatively whether waiting would let the opportunity pass.
Whether the committee prefers B006 with a contested third name to B047 with a clean credit. I do not know how I would settle the Hasan or Mele question and defer to the condensed-matter members.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure: I spent a year in John Hall's laboratory during my PhD, and Jun Ye is associated with Hall's JILA group. This is a distant scientific lineage and not a collaboration, and I regard it as non-disqualifying for B047, but the committee should know. I am in the WACQT leadership, which overlaps institutionally with Johansson's Chalmers base and touches B038, which I list as an alternative. I am on the management team of a Lund spin-off, Deep Light Vision, working in a different field from all shortlisted candidates. No new conflicts arose in the first round.
